title: We thank you
hookLine: everyone bows at "we give thanks"; the rabbis say this blessing is said by all
carry: no one can say it for you

lines: THE ROOM LISTENS AND ANSWERS AMEN.
cards: When the leader repeats the Amidah out loud, the congregation mostly listens. They answer amen at the end of each blessing, and let the leader speak for them. You can be represented.

Then the leader reaches one blessing, bows, and the whole room does something different. Everyone starts murmuring their own words, at the same time, quietly, as if to say: no, this one, I'll do myself.

teach.h: FOR OUR LIVES, IN YOUR HAND.
teach.b: After a short blessing asking that prayer be accepted, called Retzeh, comes the eighteenth: Modim. It begins: we thank You, for You are the Lord our God and the God of our ancestors forever.
Then it lists: for our lives, entrusted to Your hand. For our souls, in Your keeping.

teach.h: MIRACLES EVERY DAY: EVENING, MORNING, NOON.
teach.b: For Your miracles that are with us every day, and Your wonders and goodness at every time: evening, morning and noon. Not the parting of the sea. The miracles of every day.

People bow at its first word and at its end, as they did at the start of the Amidah. And when the leader repeats it aloud, the congregation says its own quiet version, called Modim d'Rabbanan, the Modim of the rabbis.

teach.h: NO ONE CAN THANK FOR YOU.
teach.b: The Talmud, in Sotah 40a, collects the words several rabbis said here, and later commentators explain why everyone joins in: someone else can make a request for you, but no one can say thank you on your behalf.

The word modim can mean both we thank and we acknowledge. In Genesis, when Leah has her fourth son, she says, in the old Jewish translation: "This time will I praise the LORD." And she names him Yehudah, Judah.
The word Jew, tradition notes, goes back to Judah.
So in a sense, the very name of the people is a thank-you. On Hanukkah and Purim, a paragraph about those miracles is added right here.

how: Jews bow at the beginning and end of Modim, the thanksgiving blessing of every Amidah; during the leader's repetition the congregation says Modim d'Rabbanan quietly, and on Hanukkah and Purim the paragraph Al hanissim is added.

o: a hymn praising God for the Exodus
we thank, we acknowledge: the bowing blessing
a blessing asking that prayer be accepted

s: the congregation lets the leader say Modim for them
they say their own quiet version: no one can thank on your behalf.
the blessing thanks God for miracles of every day

games.q: the leader is repeating the Amidah aloud. you've answered amen to every blessing. now the leader reaches Modim. what do you do?
o: say your own quiet Modim, and bow.
games.why: the congregation says Modim d'Rabbanan: someone can ask for you, but no one can thank for you.

practice: Count three ordinary things from today, one from the morning, one from the afternoon, one from now: a cup of coffee, a message from a friend, your lungs working without being asked.
For each one, bow your head slightly, a small nod, the way you might to someone across a room. If you pray, you can say: we thank You.

wordCard.voice: Modim. We thank, we acknowledge. The Amidah's thanksgiving blessing, said with a bow, by everyone in their own words.

orig.note: Hebrew: we thank, we acknowledge. from y-d-h, the root of Yehudah, Judah.

carryVoice: Your line: no one can say it for you. The miracles of every day count too. See you tomorrow.
